title: Oops Reversal
teaches: The Oops as we trade it: one daily candle in a leader after an orderly pullback, that opens under the prior close, trades under the prior day's low and closes back over the prior close, with a Super Oops closing over the prior high; the buy is a market order as price trades back over the prior close after the undercut, the stop sits a few cents under the Oops day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R, a close back under the prior close is a warning and the stop is the exit.

questions.why: True. The main Oops day passes three tests. It opens under the prior close, trades under the prior day's low and closes back over the prior close. Williams' version also needs an open under the prior low. A Super Oops also closes over the prior high. Neither extra is needed for the main version.
questions.lesson_line: Open under, undercut, close back over: that is the Oops.
questions.simple: True, because the main Oops opens under the prior close, dips under the prior low, then closes back over that close.

questions.why: It closes over the prior high. A Super Oops is any Oops that closes over the prior high, so the whole prior day is engulfed. A trade over that high that closes back under it does not count.
questions.lesson_line: Close over the prior high, and the Oops is a Super.

questions.q: In our scans, when does the Oops buy fill?
choices: On the reclaim, after the undercut
Right as it opens under the prior close
At the open, before any undercut
At the open of the next session
questions.answer: On the reclaim, after the undercut
questions.why: Our scans buy as price trades back over the prior close, once the day has traded under the prior low. It is a market order when that trigger prints, not a resting buy-stop placed at the open. No reclaim after the undercut means no trade.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut first, then the reclaim of the close. That is our scans' buy.

wrong.Right as it opens under the prior close: An open under the prior close is only the first test. The undercut and the reclaim must follow.
wrong.At the open, before any undercut: A buy at the open can fill before the undercut. Our scans wait for the reclaim.
wrong.At the open of the next session: Our scans buy on the Oops day itself, not at the next open.

deeper.trap: Trap: calling the open under the prior close a buy. It is only the first of three tests. Our scans wait for the undercut of the prior low and then the reclaim of the prior close.

questions.lesson_line: Alert at the prior close, then a market order. No resting stop at the open.
questions.simple: False, because we buy at market when the trigger prints. A resting buy-stop at the open can fill before the undercut.

deeper.trap: Trap: a resting buy-stop feels careful because you do not have to watch. But it is live from the open. If price reaches its level before the day has traded under the prior low, it fills with no undercut behind it. Set an alert at the prior close and buy at market when the trigger prints.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The prior close sits ___% to 12% below the 20-day high.
questions.why: 3%. The prior close should sit 3% to 12% under the 20-day high, which is the highest high of the 20 sessions before. Under 3% is not a real pullback, with little to reverse from. Past 12% is outside the range too.
questions.lesson_line: A real pullback first: 3% to 12% off the 20-day high.
questions.simple: The pullback must be at least 3% off the 20-day high, and not past 12%.

questions.q: An Oops can fire on a dip of under 1% from the 20-day high.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A real pullback comes first, 3% to 12% off the 20-day high. A dip at the highs has nothing to reverse from.
questions.lesson_line: No pullback, nothing to reverse.

questions.q: What should the Oops-day low tag?
choices: A rising 21-day or 50-day average
The 5-day average, a faster read
The 10-day average, our trail line
The 100-day average, a middle line
questions.answer: A rising 21-day or 50-day average
questions.why: The Oops-day low should sit within 0.5 ATR of the rising 21-day EMA or 50-day SMA. Or it should undercut a visible level. That could be a flag low, a double-bottom low, a gap-support level, a high-volume close or a round number. The undercut should tag something the market can see.
questions.lesson_line: The undercut should tag something the market can see.

wrong.The 5-day average, a faster read: The card names the rising 21-day EMA or 50-day SMA, or a visible level. A 5-day average is not on that list.
wrong.The 10-day average, our trail line: The 10-day is our trail for fast movers, not where the Oops-day low should tag. The card names the 21-day EMA or 50-day SMA.
wrong.The 100-day average, a middle line: The card names the rising 21-day EMA or 50-day SMA. A 100-day average is not on that list.

questions.simple: The low should tag a rising 21-day or 50-day average, or a clear level. The undercut needs something the market can see.

questions.q: The Oops needs a red prior day.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A red prior day is preferred, not required. Three tests decide an Oops. They are the open under the prior close, the undercut of the prior low and the close back over. A red prior day is not one of them.
questions.lesson_line: Red prior day: preferred. Not required.
questions.simple: False, because a red prior day is preferred but the Oops does not need one.

questions.q: How big should the Oops day be?
choices: Under 3 ATR, a technical candle
At least 3 ATR, to show real force
A news-sized bar; bigger is better
Size does not matter for an Oops
questions.answer: Under 3 ATR, a technical candle
questions.why: Under 3 ATR, a technical candle. The rule asks for a technical Oops day, not a news day, with the day's range under 3 ATR. That is a ceiling, not a floor. A dramatic, news-sized Oops day is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: A clear but technical candle, not a news bar.

wrong.At least 3 ATR, to show real force: The rule is a ceiling of 3 ATR, not a floor.
wrong.A news-sized bar; bigger is better: A dramatic, news-sized Oops day is a named mistake.
wrong.Size does not matter for an Oops: Size matters. The rule keeps the day's range under 3 ATR.

questions.simple: Keep the Oops day's range under 3 ATR, so it is a normal candle and not a big news bar.

reasons: a threshold from the card that is still proposed

questions.q: A volume surge is required for an Oops.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. There is no volume requirement for the Oops. The tests are the open under the prior close, the undercut of the prior low and the close back over. Volume is not one of them.
questions.lesson_line: No volume test here. The undercut and the reclaim are the test.
questions.simple: False, because our Oops rules have no volume test, so the open, the undercut and the close decide it.

questions.q: How much comes off at the first trim, 3R?
choices: A third
Half
All of it
A quarter
questions.answer: A third
questions.why: A third. The hard rule is a third at 3R, another third at 5R, then trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, and trail the last third.

wrong.Half: The hard rule is a third, not half.
wrong.All of it: Trims are thirds. The last third is trailed.
wrong.A quarter: The hard rule is a third at 3R.

questions.q: Bought at 149.22 with the stop at 146.52. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 157.32. One R is the fill minus the stop, 149.22 minus 146.52. Add three of those to the fill to get 3R. The first third comes off there.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: 3R is 157.32, which is the fill plus three times the distance down to the stop.

deeper.example: Example: DELL on 2026-03-19. The buy was 149.22 and the stop 146.52, a stop 1.81% away. 3R came the next day.

questions.q: A phone alert set at the Oops-day low can replace the stop order, if you act on it.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. An alert is only a message. It does not sell for you, and acting on it depends on you seeing it and deciding in time. The stop order sits a few cents under the Oops-day low.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False, because an alert only tells you the price is there, while a stop order with the broker actually sells.

questions.q: What floor must an Oops stock clear?
choices: $10 and $20 million a day
$5 and $5 million a day
$20 and $10 million a day
$10 and 1 million shares a day
questions.answer: $10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million a day. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Thin stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars a share, twenty million a day. Below that, no Oops.

wrong.$5 and $5 million a day: Too low. Our floor is $10 a share and $20 million a day.
wrong.$20 and $10 million a day: Swapped. The share price floor is $10 and the daily dollar floor is $20 million.
wrong.$10 and 1 million shares a day: The daily floor is $20 million traded, not a count of shares.

questions.simple: Our floor is a price of at least $10 and at least $20 million traded a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23) and a held decision (D-030)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Never buy an Oops more than ___% above the prior close.
questions.why: 4%. We never buy more than 4% above the prior close, the buy point. Past that you are chasing. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the prior close and I am done.
questions.simple: Never pay more than 4% over the prior close, because past that you are chasing.

questions.q: Why does the stop sit under the Oops-day low?
choices: It marks where the trap was set
It keeps the loss at exactly 3%
It is the prior day's low
It is the low of the last 20 days
questions.answer: It marks where the trap was set
questions.why: It marks where the trap was set. A trade below the Oops-day low is the stop, and the stop is the exit. It is not a fixed percent. The stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy, but the Oops-day low sets it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the Oops-day low the trap has failed. That is the exit.

wrong.It keeps the loss at exactly 3%: About 3% is only where the stop usually sits. The Oops-day low sets it.
wrong.It is the prior day's low: The Oops day already traded under the prior day's low. The stop goes under the Oops-day low.
wrong.It is the low of the last 20 days: That is not a rule. The stop goes under the Oops-day low, where the trap was set.

questions.simple: The stop sits there because that low is where the trap was set, so a trade below it means the trap failed.

deeper.trap: Trap: treating the 3% as the stop. Our rule says the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. That describes where it tends to land, not how to place it. Place it a few cents under the Oops-day low.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A13)

questions.q: A Super Oops only needs the day's high to pass the prior high.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A Super Oops is any Oops that closes over the prior high, so the whole prior day is engulfed. A trade over the prior high during the day is not enough. The Super close is a grade mark, not a guarantee.
questions.lesson_line: The Super is a close over the prior high.
questions.simple: False, because a Super Oops needs the day to close over the prior high, not just trade over it.

questions.q: The 20-day high is 100.00 and the prior close is 91.50. How far has it pulled back, in percent?
questions.why: 8.5%. The drop is 100.00 minus 91.50, divided by the 20-day high of 100.00. That sits inside the 3% to 12% range, so it is a real pullback to reverse from.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pullback from the 20-day high. Inside 3% to 12%.
questions.simple: It pulled back 8.5% from the 20-day high, which is inside the 3% to 12% range.

questions.q: Filled at 31.51 with the stop at 31.12. How far is the stop from the fill, in percent?
questions.why: 1.24%. The distance is the fill minus the stop, divided by the fill, times 100. That is well inside the 3% where the stop usually sits. About 3% is the usual reach, not a hard cap, and the Oops-day low still sets the stop. This is the ACN trade.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop as a percent of the fill. About 3% is the usual reach.
questions.simple: The stop is 1.24% below the fill, well inside the 3% our stops usually stay within.

deeper.counter: Counter-example: DELL on 2026-03-19 had a deeper undercut, so its stop was wider. The buy was 149.22 and the stop 146.52, which is 1.81% away. That is still inside about 3%, but a wider stop means fewer shares for the same risk.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-005, stop width)

questions.q: By our main test, is it an Oops day?
choices: Yes, it passes all three tests
No, it opened over the prior low
Yes, but only as a Super Oops
No, the undercut was too shallow
questions.story: Yesterday: high 50.60, low 49.40, close 50.00. Today: open 49.70, low 49.10, close 50.30.
questions.answer: Yes, it passes all three tests
questions.why: Yes. Test one: the 49.70 open is under the 50.00 prior close. Test two: the 49.10 low is under the 49.40 prior low. Test three: the 50.30 close is over the 50.00 prior close. The close stays under the 50.60 prior high, so it is a plain Oops, not a Super. Williams' version would also need an open under 49.40.
questions.lesson_line: Check the three tests one by one against yesterday.

wrong.No, the undercut was too shallow: Any trade under the prior low counts as the undercut.
wrong.No, it opened over the prior low: That is Williams' stricter version. The main version needs an open under the prior close.
wrong.Yes, but only as a Super Oops: It closed at 50.30, under the prior high of 50.60, so it is not a Super Oops. A plain Oops still counts.

questions.simple: Yes. It opened under the prior close, dipped under the prior low and closed back over that close.

reasons: every number is in the story

questions.q: What do you call it?
choices: It is a Super Oops setup
It is a Williams Oops setup
It is a plain Oops, no Super
It is a Kicker gap setup
questions.story: Yesterday: high 50.60, low 49.40, close 50.00. Today opens at 49.70, trades down to 49.10 and closes at 50.80.
questions.answer: It is a Super Oops setup
questions.why: A Super Oops. It opened at 49.70, under the prior close of 50.00. It traded down to 49.10, under the prior low of 49.40. It closed at 50.80, over the prior close. It also closed over the prior high of 50.60, which makes it a Super. It opened over the prior low, so it is not a Williams open.
questions.lesson_line: Close over the prior high makes it a Super.

wrong.It is a Williams Oops setup: It opened at 49.70, over the prior low of 49.40. Williams opens under the prior low.
wrong.It is a plain Oops, no Super: It closed at 50.80, over the prior high of 50.60, which makes it a Super.
wrong.It is a Kicker gap setup: A Kicker gaps up over a red day's close. This opened under the prior close.

questions.simple: A Super Oops is an Oops that closes over the prior high, and this one closed above it.

deeper.trap: Check the open against the right line. Williams needs an open under the prior low of 49.40. This day opened at 49.70, over it, so it is our main Oops with a Super close, not Williams' own version.

reasons: the Williams open is a held decision (D-104), only the originator's definition is used

questions.q: In our scans, which move fills the buy?
choices: The 11:00 move back over 50.00
The 9:40 touch back up to 50.00
Both, since each reached 50.00
Neither; buy at the next day's open
questions.story: The prior close is 50.00 and the prior low 49.40. The stock opens under 50.00 and touches it at 9:40, then breaks 49.40. At 11:00 it trades back over 50.00.
questions.answer: The 11:00 move back over 50.00
questions.why: The 11:00 move, after the undercut. By then the stock had broken the prior low of 49.40. Trading back over 50.00 is the reclaim our scans buy. The 9:40 touch came before the undercut, and buying that touch is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut first. A touch before it is not the trigger.

wrong.The 9:40 touch back up to 50.00: That touch came before the undercut. A touch of the prior close before the undercut is not a trigger.
wrong.Both, since each reached 50.00: Only the move after the undercut counts.
wrong.Neither; buy at the next day's open: Our scans buy on the Oops day itself, as a market order when the trigger prints.

questions.simple: Our scans buy on the 11:00 move, because it comes after the stock traded under the prior low.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the entry trigger)

questions.q: Do you buy it now?
choices: No, over 4% above the prior close
Yes, a strong Oops often continues
Yes, with a smaller stop to fit
No, it needs a Super close first
questions.story: The prior close is 50.00. You missed the reclaim. At 11:30 the stock is at 52.30.
questions.answer: No, over 4% above the prior close
questions.why: No. 52.30 is more than 4% above the prior close of 50.00, so buying now is a chase. Our rule is no buy more than 4% above the prior close. You missed this one, so let it go.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the prior close, you missed it. Let it go.

wrong.Yes, a strong Oops often continues: Strength is not a reason to chase. Past 4% over the prior close, there is no buy.
wrong.Yes, with a smaller stop to fit: The stop stays a few cents under the Oops-day low. Past 4% over the prior close, there is no buy to size.
wrong.No, it needs a Super close first: A plain Oops is still an Oops, and a Super close is a grade mark, not a requirement. The block here is the 4% limit.

questions.simple: No. The stock is already more than 4% above the prior close, so buying now is chasing.

reasons: rests on the owner's no-chase rule (C28)

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: No, a report is inside 3 days
Yes, it is an Oops, not earnings
No, earnings days are never traded
Yes, then sell before the report
questions.story: A clean Oops reclaims the prior close. The company reports earnings in two days.
questions.answer: No, a report is inside 3 days
questions.why: No. We make no new Oops buy in the 3 days before a report, and this one reports in two days. The rule bars the buy itself, so a plan to sell before the report does not change it. A position goes through a report only if the trade is already up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report.

wrong.Yes, it is an Oops, not earnings: The report window is its own rule.
wrong.Yes, then sell before the report: The rule is no new buys inside the window.
wrong.No, earnings days are never traded: An earnings-day Oops is allowed but grades lower. The block here is the report inside 3 days.

questions.simple: No. We make no new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this company reports in two days.

reasons: rests on the owner's earnings rule (B22)

questions.q: A big red bar, a drop of over 4%, came three days before. What does it do to the Oops?
choices: It removes it from our list
Nothing, it is old history now
It only counts if it was a gap
It raises the grade a little
questions.answer: It removes it from our list
questions.why: It removes it from our list. The pullback should be orderly. No bar in the 5 sessions before may drop over 4% or have a range over 2.5 ATR. A drop of over 4% three days earlier breaks that. Buying after one is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: An orderly drift only. A big red bar in the days before is out.

wrong.Nothing, it is old history now: Three days is inside the 5 sessions the rule looks back over.
wrong.It only counts if it was a gap: The rule counts a drop over 4% or a range over 2.5 ATR, gap or not.
wrong.It raises the grade a little: A big red bar in the days before does not help. The card puts the stock off the list.

questions.simple: A drop of over 4% in the five sessions before breaks the orderly pullback, so the stock comes off the list.

reasons: thresholds from the card that are still proposed

questions.q: Your move at the close?
choices: Hold to the stop; do not add
Sell at the close, it has failed
Add a second lot on the dip
Move the stop under 31.30
questions.story: You bought the reclaim of the 31.50 prior close at 31.52, the way our scans do, with the stop at 31.12. The day closes at 31.30, back under the prior close, above your stop.
questions.answer: Hold to the stop; do not add
questions.why: Hold to the stop and do not add. The day closed at 31.30, back under the prior close of 31.50, so the trade is wrong as an Oops. But the stop is the exit, and 31.12 has not traded. Treat the next day's open below the prior close as a warning.
questions.lesson_line: A close back under the prior close means the Oops failed. Hold to the stop and do not add.

wrong.Add a second lot on the dip: We never add after a failed reclaim. The full size goes in at one price.
wrong.Move the stop under 31.30: The card says to hold to the Oops-day stop after a failed reclaim.
wrong.Sell at the close, it has failed: The stop is the exit, not a weak close.

questions.simple: Hold to the stop and do not add, because the stop is the exit even after a weak close.

deeper.trap: Trap: a weak close feels like a reason to act. A close under the prior close tells you the trade is wrong as an Oops. But the Oops-day stop still decides the exit. Do not sell early and do not add. Treat the next day's open below the prior close as the warning.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the entry trigger)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Nothing; the stop is the plan
Wish you had used a wider stop
Skip the stop and hold next time
Decide the setup no longer works
questions.story: You bought at 67.48 with the stop at 66.70. The next day it opens at 68.48, then sells straight through your stop to 66.63.
questions.answer: Nothing; the stop is the plan
questions.why: Nothing. A perfect-looking day gives no warning, and the stop is the whole plan. This was ADBE on 2014-03-12. It opened at 68.48, over the buy, and sold straight through the Oops-day low. The stop took a small planned loss, 1.16% from the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A perfect-looking Oops gives no warning. The stop is the plan.

wrong.Wish you had used a wider stop: A wider stop is a bigger loss. The stop did its job.
wrong.Skip the stop and hold next time: The stop is the exit, and every position has a real stop order with the broker.
wrong.Decide the setup no longer works: One stop-out is not a verdict. A good example can have a horrible result, and the stop is the whole plan.

questions.simple: Do nothing. The stop did its job, and a perfect-looking Oops can still fail with no warning.

deeper.trap: Do not judge the trade by the result. The stop sat 1.16% under the 67.48 buy, a small planned loss. ADBE then fell to 59.63 by 04-07, so a wider stop would only have lost more.

reasons: a dated example read off our own bars

questions.q: Under our gap rule, where is the stop now?
choices: 30.85, the first 30-minute low
31.12, the original stop price
Out at once; the loss is past 2R
The open, 30.95, the gap price
questions.story: You bought at 31.52 with the stop at 31.12. The next morning it gaps open at 30.95. The first 30-minute low is 30.85.
questions.answer: 30.85, the first 30-minute low
questions.why: 30.85. A gap down through the stop hands the decision to the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. The loss at that low is under 2R, so the ceiling does not force an exit. This is the one exception to a stop that only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.31.12, the original stop price: The stop is already through. The 30-minute low is the new stop.
wrong.Out at once; the loss is past 2R: The loss at the 30-minute low is inside the 2R ceiling.
wrong.The open, 30.95, the gap price: The open is not the decision. The 30-minute low is.

questions.simple: The new stop is the low of the first 30 minutes, 30.85, because the gap went through the old stop.

deeper.trap: The gap price is not the decision. The open at 30.95 only tells you the gap happened. The first 30-minute bar sets the stop, and if its low had taken the loss past 2R, the rule is to get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's gap rule (B20)
the 2R check is arithmetic done by the cold checker, not a calc

questions.q: What does our plan call for at 3R?
choices: Sell a third, stop to breakeven
Sell it all and lock in the 3R
Sell half, leave the stop alone
Hold all, nudge the stop up
questions.story: You bought at 149.22 with the stop at 146.52. The Oops reaches 3R.
questions.answer: Sell a third, stop to breakeven
questions.why: Sell a third and move the stop to breakeven. The hard rule is a third at 3R. Our plans move the stop on what is left to breakeven at the first trim. The rulebook's ideal window for breakeven is 2R to 5R, so 3R fits it. Another third comes off at 5R, then the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: At 3R sell a third and lift the stop to breakeven.

wrong.Sell it all and lock in the 3R: Trims are thirds, and the last third is trailed.
wrong.Sell half, leave the stop alone: The hard rule is a third.
wrong.Hold all, nudge the stop up: The first third comes off at 3R.

questions.simple: At 3R we sell one third and move the stop up to breakeven, as our plan does by default.

reasons: held decision D-019 on the breakeven

questions.q: When do you take the first trim?
choices: Right away, at the open
At the close, if it holds
On a dip back to 52.40
After the first 30-minute bar closes
questions.story: You hold an Oops with a 3R level of 52.40. The next morning the stock opens at 53.10.
questions.answer: Right away, at the open
questions.why: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. Your 3R level is 52.40 and the stock opened at 53.10, past it, so the first third comes off right there. Do not wait for the close or for a dip.
questions.lesson_line: Open past the level, take the trim at the open.

wrong.At the close, if it holds: The rule is to take it at the open, not to wait for the close.
wrong.On a dip back to 52.40: The stock already opened past 52.40. Take the trim at the open, because the dip may never come.
wrong.After the first 30-minute bar closes: The first 30 minutes decide a gap against the stop. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

questions.simple: Take the first third at the open, because the stock opened at 53.10, past the 3R level of 52.40.

questions.q: Your move now?
choices: Sell it and find a new setup
Hold on and wait for the 5R trim
Add more on a break of the range
Widen the stop for more room
questions.story: Ten trading days are done. The Oops has chopped sideways at +0.5R. The stop has not been touched.
questions.answer: Sell it and find a new setup
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. At +0.5R after ten days the Oops has not reached 1R, so the time stop applies. Holding for 5R, adding or widening the stop are all off the plan.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and under 1R: sell and use the money elsewhere.

wrong.Hold on and wait for the 5R trim: A trade under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
wrong.Add more on a break of the range: We buy the full size once, at one price. No adding.

questions.simple: Sell it, because a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold to free the money.

deeper.example: Example: the story's trade sits at +0.5R after ten days. Holding for 5R keeps the money tied up in a trade that has not reached 1R. Selling frees it for the next setup.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-019, the time stop)

questions.q: Williams' exit, the first profitable open, is our exit.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Williams' bailout exits on the first profitable open, even for 1c of profit. Ours is a third at 3R, a third at 5R and a trail on the last third.
questions.lesson_line: Williams' exit is his. Ours is thirds and a trail.
questions.simple: No. Williams sells at the first profitable open, but our plan sells a third at 3R and a third at 5R.

reasons: the Williams half rests on a Radge page that blocked this run's fetch
rests on the owner's exit plan (E51)

questions.q: Which Oops longs may you take here?
choices: Only an A+ Oops, nothing less
Any A or A+ Oops, at full risk
Any Oops, but at half the size
None; Orange means mostly cash
questions.story: A clean Oops reclaims the prior close, but the market reading is Orange.
questions.answer: Only an A+ Oops, nothing less
questions.why: Only an A+ Oops. In an Orange market, only A+ setups. Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Red is mostly cash and shorts. Orange does not mean no trades, and it does not mean full size.
questions.lesson_line: Orange market, A+ only. Yellow, smaller. Green, full.

wrong.Any A or A+ Oops, at full risk: Orange takes only A+ setups, so an A is not enough. Full risk is for Green.
wrong.Any Oops, but at half the size: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Orange takes only A+ setups.
wrong.None; Orange means mostly cash: Mostly cash is Red. Orange still allows an A+.

questions.simple: In an Orange market you take only A+ setups, so you pass on any Oops that grades lower.

questions.q: Which average is the default trail for a steadier name?
choices: The 21-day
The 50-day
The 200-day
The 10-day
questions.answer: The 21-day
questions.why: The 21-day. Our default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. Sell on a close below it. After the thirds at 3R and 5R, the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 10-day. Steadier name, 21-day. Sell on a close below.

wrong.The 50-day: Our default trails are the 10-day and the 21-day, not the 50-day.
wrong.The 200-day: Our default trails are the 10-day and the 21-day, not the 200-day.
wrong.The 10-day: That is the fast-mover trail. Steadier names trail the 21-day.

questions.q: Which setup is it?

A 2B, it reclaimed the same day

A Kicker, it opened over the close
questions.story: Yesterday: low 83.10, close 83.90. Today opens at 83.50, trades under 83.10 and closes at 84.40. There is no older swing low nearby.
questions.answer: An Oops, judged on yesterday's low
questions.why: An Oops. The day opened under the prior close, broke yesterday's low and reclaimed the prior close in one candle. An Oops breaks yesterday's low and is judged on one candle. A 2B breaks a swing low, and may take up to 3 sessions to close back above it. No older swing low is near here.
questions.lesson_line: Count the age of the broken low. Yesterday's low is an Oops.

wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed the same day: A 2B breaks a swing low, not yesterday's low.
wrong.A U&R, it undercut a key level: A U&R needs a bigger level than yesterday's low. This broke yesterday's low and reclaimed the prior close the same day.
wrong.A Kicker, it opened over the close: A Kicker gaps UP over a red day's close. This opened under the prior close.

questions.simple: It is an Oops because it broke only yesterday's low and reclaimed the prior close in one day.

deeper.counter: Same shape, different level. Had it broken an older swing low and closed back over it within 3 sessions, it would be a 2B. Breaking only yesterday's low and reclaiming the close in one candle is an Oops.

questions.q: Is it an Oops?

Yes, it reclaimed within 3 sessions
Yes, it broke a low and reclaimed it
No, that is a Red to Green setup
questions.story: On Monday the stock breaks a swing low from twelve sessions ago. It closes back above that low on Tuesday. Tuesday never trades under Monday's low.
questions.answer: No, it is a 2B on an older low
questions.why: No, it is a 2B. The break was of a swing low from twelve sessions ago, not yesterday's low. An Oops breaks yesterday's low and is judged on one candle. A 2B breaks a swing low, and may take up to 3 sessions to close back above it. This one closed back over it on the next session.
questions.lesson_line: One candle is an Oops. An older low and a day or two is a 2B.

wrong.Yes, it reclaimed within 3 sessions: A 2B may take up to 3 sessions. An Oops is judged on one candle.
wrong.Yes, it broke a low and reclaimed it: An Oops is judged on one candle and yesterday's low.
wrong.No, that is a Red to Green setup: A Red to Green is only the trade back through the prior close. This reclaimed an older swing low, which is the 2B tell.

questions.simple: It broke a low from twelve sessions ago, so it is a 2B and not a one-candle Oops.

deeper.trap: The reclaim looks like an Oops, so count two things: how old the broken low is and how many candles it took. An older swing low plus a day or two to close back above it is a 2B, and a 2B may take up to 3 sessions.

reasons: the tell between lookalikes comes from the criteria cards

An Oops
A Kicker
A 2B

questions.answer: A U&R

questions.lesson_line: A bigger level and a few days: U&R. Yesterday's low in one day: Oops.

wrong.A Kicker: A Kicker gaps up. This is a dip under an average.
wrong.An Oops: An Oops must trade under the prior day's low and be judged on one candle. This stock did not.

questions.simple: It is a U&R, because the level it dipped under is a rising average, a bigger level than yesterday's low.

deeper.trap: Trap: the speed of the reclaim. Closing back above the level the next day looks like an Oops. But an Oops must trade under the prior day's low in one candle. The level is the tell. Yesterday's low is an Oops. An older swing low is a 2B. A bigger level, like the rising 50-day in this story, is a U&R.

questions.q: Which setup is it?
choices: A Kicker, it opened over the close
An Oops, it closed over the prior high
A 2B, it closed back over a swing low
A Red to Green, it turned green today
questions.story: Yesterday was a red day: it opened at 52.00, closed at 50.00 and its high was 52.40. Today the stock opens at 50.90 and closes at 52.80.
questions.answer: A Kicker, it opened over the close
questions.why: A Kicker. A Kicker gaps UP over a red day's close and is bought through the red day's high. An Oops opens DOWN under the prior close, trades under the prior low and is bought back through the prior close. Here the stock opened at 50.90, over the red close of 50.00. It cannot be an Oops, even though it closed above that day's high.
questions.lesson_line: The gap direction decides it. Up is a Kicker. Down is an Oops.

wrong.An Oops, it closed over the prior high: An Oops opens down under the prior close. This opened over it.
wrong.A 2B, it closed back over a swing low: A 2B breaks a swing low first. Nothing here says it did.
wrong.A Red to Green, it turned green today: A Red to Green is a trade back through the prior close. This opened over it, so it did not start red.

questions.simple: A gap up over a red day's close is a Kicker, and an Oops opens down instead.

deeper.trap: The close over the prior high tempts you to say Oops. But an Oops opens down under the prior close. The direction of the gap is the first test.

reasons: the tell between lookalikes comes from the criteria card

questions.q: Which setup does this day show?

An Oops, it closed over the close

questions.lesson_line: Check if it traded under yesterday's low first. If not, it is a Red to Green.

wrong.An Oops, it closed over the close: An Oops needs a trade under the prior low first.
wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low: A 2B breaks a swing low first. Nothing here says it did.
wrong.A Kicker, it reclaimed the close: A Kicker gaps UP over a red day's close. This opened under the prior close.

questions.simple: The stock never traded under yesterday's low, so it is a Red to Green and not an Oops.

questions.q: Oops or Go Signal?
choices: A Go Signal, it fires on the hourly
An Oops, it undercut a slight range
A Kicker, it gapped up over a close
A 2B, it broke and reclaimed a low
questions.story: After a catalyst gap, a stock digests in an hourly flag. It undercuts a slight range and goes red to green in the first hour.
questions.answer: A Go Signal, it fires on the hourly
questions.why: A Go Signal. A Go Signal is an hourly flag that undercuts a slight range and goes red to green in the first hour. The Oops is the daily candle's reclaim of the prior close after an undercut of the prior day's low. The chart that fires it tells them apart.
questions.lesson_line: The chart that fires it decides. Daily candle is the Oops. Hourly flag is the Go Signal.

wrong.An Oops, it undercut a slight range: The Oops is read on the daily candle, not an hourly flag.
wrong.A Kicker, it gapped up over a close: A Kicker is a daily gap up over a red day.
wrong.A 2B, it broke and reclaimed a low: A 2B breaks a swing low. This undercut a slight range inside an hourly flag.

questions.simple: This fires on an hourly flag, so it is a Go Signal, while an Oops is read on the daily candle.

deeper.trap: Red to green appears in both. A Go Signal goes red to green inside an hourly flag after a catalyst gap. An Oops is one daily candle that undercuts the prior day's low and reclaims the prior close. Same words, different chart.

reasons: the tell between lookalikes comes from the criteria card

questions.q: Is it an Oops?
choices: No, it is a delayed reaction
Yes, it passes all three tests
Yes, a news drop makes it stronger
No, the undercut is too shallow

questions.answer: No, it is a delayed reaction

questions.lesson_line: A reversal after a news bar is not an Oops.

wrong.Yes, it passes all three tests: The three tests pass, but the prior day was a news bar. That is not an orderly pullback.
wrong.Yes, a news drop makes it stronger: A big drop in the days before takes the stock off the list. It does not help.
wrong.No, the undercut is too shallow: Any trade under the prior low is an undercut. What fails here is the news day before.

questions.simple: The prior day was a big news drop, so this reversal is a delayed reaction and not an Oops.

deeper.trap: All three tests pass, so it looks like an Oops. The problem is the day before: a 6.71% fall on news. PANW's undercut was only 12 cents and its close was just 0.5% over the prior close. The day after a news day is a delayed reaction.

reasons: a dated example read off our own bars
the orderly-pullback criterion is still proposed

The undercut is missing
The close is under the prior close
The stop is over 3%

It is only a plain Oops, not a Super one
The prior day was not a red day at all
The pullback was far too deep to trade

deeper.trap: BABA's Oops-day close was 67.23 against a 200-day of 76.48. The Oops shape was clean, but shape is only one test. The 200-day rule comes first: no longs below it unless it is a parabolic long.

Yes, it opened under the close
Yes, it undercut the prior low
No, it did not close over the high

A confirmed new uptrend
A wider stop on day two
A guarantee the stop is safe

wrong.A confirmed new uptrend: A Super close is a grade mark, not a guarantee, and it confirms no trend.
wrong.A guarantee the stop is safe: A Super close is a grade mark, not a guarantee. AMAT fell through its stop.

deeper.trap: AMAT on 2022-01-14 had the best-looking close of the set, 167.00 over the 166.53 prior high. The next day was a 9% down day through the 155.55 stop, the first of three straight down days. A grade mark does not move the stop.

The close was far too weak
The stop was far too wide

questions.q: Hidden ticker, yesterday's close. Green market, no report in 3 days. Tomorrow it undercuts the low and reclaims the close. Take it?

Pass; there is no real pullback
Pass; a big news bar came first
Take it; buy the open before the dip

Take it; the 200-day is rising
Pass; the undercut is too shallow

wrong.Take it; the 200-day is rising: A rising 200-day is a plus, not a substitute for the pullback.

questions.lesson_line: A whole-market gap down that reverses is the best Oops day.

Not allowed; earnings days are out
Allowed, and it grades the same
A delayed reaction, not an Oops

questions.q: Our cap is 1% of a stock's average daily volume. It averages 800,000 shares a day. What is the most shares we hold?
questions.why: 8,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 800,000 is 8,000. A thin stock is not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Take 1% of the average daily volume. That is the most we hold.
questions.simple: We hold at most 8,000 shares, which is 1% of the stock's 800,000 shares of average daily volume.

questions.q: Our holding in a stock stays at or under 1% of its average daily volume.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. Illiquid stocks are not even watched. The cap applies to every stock, not only small ones.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of average daily volume is our ceiling. Thin stocks are skipped.
questions.simple: True, because we never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

questions.q: We skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. If that average is 80.00, what is the most we pay?
questions.why: 88.00. We skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. 80.00 plus 10% is 88.00. This is a different rule from the 4% limit above the prior close.
questions.lesson_line: No more than 10% over the 10-day average. Past that, skip.
questions.simple: The most we pay is 88.00, which is the 10-day average of 80.00 plus 10%.

questions.q: Bought at 31.51 with the stop at 31.12. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 33.46. One R is the fill minus the stop, 31.51 minus 31.12. Add five of those to the fill to get 5R. The second third comes off there, and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 5R too. The second third comes off there.
questions.simple: 5R is 33.46, which is the fill plus five times the distance down to the stop.

questions.q: What do you do now?
choices: Sell a second third, trail the rest
Sell everything that is left now
Hold it all; the trail does the work
Add a third; the stock is working
questions.story: You sold a third at 3R. Now the Oops reaches 5R.
questions.answer: Sell a second third, trail the rest
questions.why: Sell a second third and trail the last third. After the first third at 3R comes another third at 5R. Then the last third rides the trail. The plan is adjustable. We buy the full size once, so there is no adding.
questions.lesson_line: At 5R the second third comes off. The last third rides the trail.

wrong.Add a third; the stock is working: We buy the full size once, at one price. No adding.

questions.story: The prior close is 50.00 and the prior low 49.40. The stock opens at 49.70 and trades down to 49.10. It bounces and closes at 49.85, never trading over 50.00.
choices: No trade; the reclaim never came
Buy the close; 49.85 is near enough
No trade; it never broke the prior low
Buy now; the undercut is the signal
questions.answer: No trade; the reclaim never came
questions.why: No trade. The stock broke the 49.40 prior low but never traded back over the 50.00 prior close. An Oops is bought back through the prior close, so the buy never came. The 49.85 close is also under 50.00, so the day is not an Oops at all. Our card also lists this as a no-trade, a rule still marked proposed.

wrong.Buy now; the undercut is the signal: The undercut only sets the trap. The buy comes when price trades back through the prior close after it.
wrong.No trade; it never broke the prior low: It did break it. The 49.10 low is under the 49.40 prior low. What never came is the trade back over 50.00.
